passage:
I'm Ujjwal, and I live on the second floor, so I see our colony lane every day. After a TV channel ran a dramatic story about a child snatched from a park in another city, our colony changed overnight. Parents stopped sending kids to the park at all. Damini, from the flat opposite, put up a notice about strangers and started a night-watch group. I can't know what everyone felt, but the lane went strangely quiet.
What didn't change: delivery bikes still raced through our narrow lane, and kids still ran across it to buy chips. On Thursday a scooter clipped a boy's elbow. I walked him home to his mother, who took him to the clinic. Nobody put up a notice about that.

qa.q: What clipped a boy's elbow on Thursday?
qa.a: A scooter.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling as the lane went quiet?
qa.a: Ujjwal seemed uneasy and puzzled, watching fear of a rare event grow while a daily danger was ignored.

qa.q: What could the colony do about the everyday risk?
qa.a: Ask for speed breakers or slow-down signs and teach children to cross carefully, alongside sensible park supervision.

qa.q: How might the children feel about losing the park?
qa.a: They may feel bored and confused, kept indoors because of a story from another city.

grounding: A resident observes one dramatic news story push a colony into over-caution about a rare danger while an everyday traffic risk is ignored.

Monday: A news video showed a lift falling in a building in another city. By evening, Ankita's building group was buzzing. Damini, the secretary, wrote: "Nobody use the lift till further notice!"
Wednesday: Elderly residents panted up six floors with groceries. Mr Bose from 5B nearly fell on the dark stairwell, where the bulb had been dead for months. The lift itself had passed its safety check in March; the certificate was pinned by the door, but nobody mentioned it.
The next Sunday: Ankita counted three dead stair bulbs, a loose railing and wet tiles near the tank. She wrote in the group: "The lift passed its check. The stairs haven't." Damini replied, "Let's fix the lights first."

qa.q: When did the lift pass its safety check?
qa.a: In March.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling as she counted the dead bulbs?
qa.a: Ankita felt frustrated and concerned, seeing the real risk on the stairs ignored while everyone feared the lift.

qa.q: Why was Ankita's message helpful?
qa.a: It pointed to the certificate and the real, common dangers, shifting attention to what actually needed fixing.

qa.q: What was Wednesday like for Mr Bose?
qa.a: He struggled up the stairs and nearly fell in the dark, likely shaken, because of fear of a rare lift failure.

grounding: Shows a resident watching one vivid news story drive a building into avoiding its lift while the everyday dangers on the stairs are ignored.

passage:
Anand, everyone in your office is scared of flying since that crash on the news? Let your Madhuri bua tell you something. When I was twenty-five, a newspaper printed a big photo of a cobra found in a baby's cradle in some faraway town. For weeks our whole mohalla shook out every sheet, every shoe, every cradle, twice a night. Mothers barely slept.
Meanwhile the open drain at the end of our lane had no cover, and children played on its edge every day. I watched it and said nothing, because I was scared of snakes too. Then one monsoon a little boy slipped in; thank God the vegetable seller pulled him out. Only then did the mohalla fix the drain cover. One photo moved us more than the danger we saw every day.

qa.q: Who pulled the boy out of the drain?
qa.a: The vegetable seller.

qa.q: What was young Madhuri feeling during those weeks?
qa.a: She felt scared along with everyone, even while noticing the open drain nobody worried about.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have come sooner?
qa.a: Covering the drain, the everyday danger, instead of only checking sheets for a rare snake.

qa.q: How might the mothers of the mohalla have felt during those weeks?
qa.a: They were anxious and exhausted, barely sleeping while shaking out sheets for a rare danger.

grounding: An aunt recalls watching a single dramatic news photo drive her neighbourhood into over-caution about a rare danger while a common one was ignored.

"Zeenat khala, send it to me. Let me look."

"But what if it happens?"
"How many children do you know who've been poisoned by bus-stop chocolates?"
"...None."
"Me neither. It's very rare. Teaching the kids not to take food from strangers is good anyway. But forwarding this will just scare Nani."
"So don't send?"
"Don't send. I'll explain in the group, gently."

qa.a: From the ladies' group.

qa.a: She felt worried and protective, anxious that the children could be in danger.

qa.q: Which checks did Parveen make before deciding?
qa.a: Looked for a date and source, traced the photo to an old unrelated story, and asked how common such cases really are.

qa.q: How might Nani have felt if the message had reached her?
qa.a: Nani would likely have felt frightened for the children over a very rare, probably false, threat.

grounding: Shows an adult tracing a scare message to its source, asking how common the danger really is, and gently stopping the chain with a worried relative.

passage:
I'm Dhruv, and last month I became the family's fact-checker. My sister Simran forwarded a video to the family group: a phone bursting into flames on a pillow, with "NEVER charge at night!!" Within an hour Papa had moved every charger to the kitchen, and Mummy was waking at 3 a.m. to check the phones.
I found the original: a single case, a cheap unbranded charger, years ago. The phone maker's safety page said problems were very rare and mostly came from damaged cables or fake chargers. I didn't forward anything. Instead, at dinner, I showed Mummy the page and said, "Use the proper charger, don't cover it with a pillow, and you can sleep."
She laughed with relief. Simran rolled her eyes, but she stopped forwarding.

qa.q: Where did Papa move every charger?
qa.a: To the kitchen.

qa.q: How did Mummy feel when Dhruv showed her the page?
qa.a: She felt relieved and laughed, freed from waking at 3 a.m. to check the phones.

qa.q: What steps did Dhruv take to stop the chain?
qa.a: Found the original single case, checked how common such problems are, didn't forward, and explained gently at dinner.

qa.q: How might Simran feel about Dhruv checking her forward?
qa.a: Simran seemed a bit annoyed, rolling her eyes, but accepted it enough to stop forwarding.

grounding: Shows an adult tracing a scary video to its source, checking how rare the danger is, and calmly explaining to worried family instead of forwarding.

Supervisor's note, district office. Swati, team lead.
On Friday a message spread across the town groups: "Old bridge has cracked, will collapse any day, don't cross!" with a blurry photo. Ojas, our youngest field officer, received it from eleven relatives. I watched how he handled it.
He did not forward it. He looked for where it began: the photo showed a different bridge, in another state, from 2019. He called the public works office, which confirmed the old bridge had been inspected in August and passed. He also noted that bridge failures like that are very rare here, while accidents on that same road are not.
Then he replied to his family group calmly: the source, the inspection date, and a request not to forward. Two uncles thanked him. He will brief the team on Monday.

qa.q: When was the old bridge inspected?
qa.a: In August.

qa.q: What might Ojas have felt receiving the message from eleven relatives?
qa.a: Ojas likely felt some pressure and concern, but stayed calm and curious enough to check before reacting.

qa.q: What steps did Ojas take before replying?
qa.a: Traced the photo to another bridge from 2019, called the public works office, and compared how rare such failures really are.

qa.q: How might the two uncles have felt after Ojas's reply?
qa.a: They likely felt relieved and grateful to have a clear source instead of fear.

grounding: A supervisor's note shows a young officer tracing a scare to its source, checking how common the risk is, and stopping the chain with a calm explanation.
